title: Nutrition · SUMS · 1st-batch retake
originalFilename: Retake final exam of Nutrition of SUMS - 1st batch.pdf
scopeNote: 40 numbered questions across 6 pages with printed answers. SUMS and 1st batch derive from the downloaded filename; the document itself says Nutrition retake examination for medical students, with no date. Three edited study versions correct overbroad/underspecified originals; one item accepts two defensible options.

questions.prompt: What is the energy density?
options: The number of calories present in each gram of food
The number of vitamins and minerals in the food
The ratio of protein to carbohydrate in the food
The total volume of food relative to its weight
questions.explanation: Energy density is food energy divided by food mass, usually kcal/g. Nutrient density is a different idea.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 29–30, 203.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a basic principle of diet planning?
questions.explanation: Adequacy, balance and moderation support a varied diet. Routine elimination of entire food groups is not a general planning principle; specific allergies or diseases require individualized substitutions.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 35–40.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: A 40-year-old man develops fat malabsorption after gastric bypass surgery. Which clinical sign is more likely?
options: Steatorrhea and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins
questions.explanation: Unabsorbed fat causes fatty stools and impairs absorption of vitamins A, D, E and K. The stem already establishes fat malabsorption.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 130–144, 210–224.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: A teenager with a diet containing soda and fast food has decreased bone density. What is the main cause?
options: Deficiency of calcium and vitamin D
questions.explanation: Insufficient calcium and vitamin D compromise bone mineralization and are the best listed explanation. Diet history alone does not establish the cause of low bone density.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 218–221, 254–257.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: Which of the following options is most likely to cause a slower glycemic response?
questions.explanation: Whole oats supply an intact food matrix and viscous beta-glucan fiber, slowing absorption compared with the listed refined or glucose-rich options.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 69–74.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: Which of the following dietary changes is more effective in reducing the risk of cardiovascular diseases related to carbohydrate consumption?
options: Replacing refined grains with whole grains
Limiting added sugars and increasing fiber intake
questions.explanation: Both replacing refined grains with whole grains and reducing added sugars while increasing fiber are sound changes. The source selects C, but its wording provides no fair basis to reject B; either is accepted.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 69–74, 576–585.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key. More than one option is defensible; either B or C is accepted.

questions.prompt: During prolonged fasting, which sequence of metabolic changes occurs?
options: Glycogen breakdown → Gluconeogenesis → Ketone body formation
Ketone body formation → Glycogen breakdown → Glycolysis
questions.explanation: Glycogenolysis initially supports glucose; gluconeogenesis becomes more important as glycogen falls, and ketone production rises with prolonged fasting. These processes overlap rather than switching on in isolation.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 158–164.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: What is the biochemical basis of symptoms in lactose intolerance?
options: Absorption of lactose into the bloodstream without digestion
Deficiency of lactase enzyme leading to fermentation of undigested lactose in the large intestine
questions.explanation: Reduced lactase leaves lactose unabsorbed. Osmotic water retention and colonic fermentation cause diarrhea, bloating and gas.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 60–62.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: Which change in dietary fats has the greatest effect on lowering LDL cholesterol levels?
options: Replacing monounsaturated fats (MUFA) with saturated fats (SFA)
Replacing trans fats with polyunsaturated fats (PUFA)
questions.explanation: Replacing industrial trans fat with unsaturated fat improves the lipid profile. The other choices do not provide an LDL-lowering substitution.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 89–99.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: A food product that remains semi-solid at room temperature and contains trans fats indicates what about its production process?
options: It is partially hydrogenated to increase shelf life
It is enriched with omega-3 fats
questions.explanation: Partial hydrogenation historically generated industrial trans fatty acids while making oils more solid and shelf stable. Natural ruminant trans fats are an exception to inferring the process from trans fat alone.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 86–89.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: How does excessive intake of saturated fats affect the lipid profile and the risk of cardiovascular diseases?
options: Increases LDL and contributes to atherosclerosis
Has no effect on lipid profile
questions.explanation: Many saturated fatty acids raise LDL relative to unsaturated-fat replacements. The clinical benefit of reducing saturated fat depends in part on what replaces it.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 91–99.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: During fasting, fat becomes the main energy source for the body. Which characteristic of fats explains their efficiency as long-term energy storage?
options: High energy content (9 kcal per gram)
questions.explanation: Fat yields approximately 9 kcal/g versus 4 for carbohydrate or protein, and triacylglycerol is stored with little water. This makes it energy dense.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 29–30.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: A patient with a normal BMI but decreased muscle mass visits. How do you expect their resting energy expenditure (REE) to compare to a healthy individual?
questions.explanation: With other factors comparable, less metabolically active fat-free mass lowers REE. Normal BMI does not demonstrate normal body composition.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 161–170, 394–395.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: A patient with a history of a strict diet and rapid weight loss has experienced a decrease in basal metabolic rate. What is the main cause of this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Loss of fat-free mass reduces basal expenditure. Adaptive thermogenesis also contributes during restriction but is not one of the choices.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 161–170.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: A patient with a history of high carbohydrate intake and obesity visits. If their respiratory quotient (RQ) is greater than 1, which metabolic state is more likely?
questions.explanation: In the stated overfeeding context, net conversion of carbohydrate to fat can produce a respiratory quotient above 1. A measured respiratory exchange ratio above 1 during intense exercise has other explanations.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 158–163.
Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed., chapter 73, respiratory quotient and conversion of carbohydrate into fat.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: A 45-year-old man with a history of hyperthyroidism has lost weight. Which mechanism plays the biggest role in this condition?
questions.explanation: Excess thyroid hormone increases basal metabolic activity and heat production, raising energy expenditure.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 161–165.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: PKU is characterized by absence or deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Classic phenylketonuria is caused by deficient phenylalanine hydroxylase activity, impairing conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 116–120.
https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/phenylketonuria/

questions.prompt: In an illustrative daily protein-turnover model, 300 g of amino acids enter protein synthesis and 60 g are supplied by the diet. What percentage is dietary?
questions.explanation: Most amino acids in protein turnover are recycled, but dietary contribution is not a universal fixed percentage. The edited study item gives explicit amounts: 60/300 × 100 = 20%.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 111–113.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key. Edited study version; original wording/options retained.

questions.prompt: Which amino acid is particularly low in cereal proteins?
questions.explanation: Lysine is commonly the limiting essential amino acid in cereal proteins; legumes can complement this limitation.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 118–121.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

options: Measurement of body length or height
questions.explanation: Anthropometry measures physical body dimensions such as height, length, weight and circumferences.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 419–425.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: According to established WHO standards, a Z-score for head circumference falling within the range of -2 to +2 is considered:
questions.explanation: This range falls within approximately two standard deviations of the age/sex reference median. Growth trajectory and clinical context still matter; a normal-range value alone does not exclude disease.
evidence: https://www.who.int/tools/child-growth-standards/standards/head-circumference-for-age
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: Kwashiorkor is a form of severe deficiency in what nutrient?
questions.explanation: Protein is the traditional exam answer. Nutritional edema/kwashiorkor is a multifactorial form of severe malnutrition, not adequately explained as isolated protein deficiency in every child.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 116–118, 424–426.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: A key sign of Kwashiorkor is:
questions.explanation: Bilateral pitting nutritional edema is the distinguishing feature; swelling can conceal loss of muscle and fat.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 116–118.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: What does the term "Marasmus" relate to a lack of?
questions.explanation: Marasmus is severe wasting from inadequate overall energy intake, usually with multiple nutrient deficits. It is not an isolated vitamin or mineral deficiency.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 116–118.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: What is the common appearance of a person with Marasmus?
questions.explanation: Severe loss of muscle and subcutaneous fat produces marked wasting. Nutritional edema points instead to edematous malnutrition or a mixed phenotype.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 116–118.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: What is another name for Vitamin A?
questions.explanation: Retinol is a preformed vitamin A compound. Vitamin A is a family of related compounds, not exclusively retinol.

questions.prompt: A deficiency of Vitamin A can lead to which condition?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency reduces availability of retinal for visual pigment, causing impaired dark adaptation and night blindness.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 212–218.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: What is another name for Vitamin D?
questions.explanation: Cholecalciferol is vitamin D3. Ergocalciferol is D2; the source uses the family name loosely.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 218–221.

questions.prompt: A deficiency of Vitamin D can lead to which bone disease in children?
questions.explanation: Inadequate vitamin D can impair growth-plate mineralization and cause rickets in children. Low dietary calcium is another cause of nutritional rickets.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 218–221.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: What is a sign of Vitamin E deficiency?
questions.explanation: Vitamin E deficiency can damage nerves and cause peripheral neuropathy and ataxia, particularly with chronic fat malabsorption or genetic disorders.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 221–223.
https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminE-HealthProfessional/
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of Vitamin K?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K supports gamma-carboxylation of clotting proteins. It also has bone-protein functions, but clotting is the principal exam answer.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 223–224.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: A deficiency of Vitamin C can lead to what disease?
questions.explanation: Vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen maturation, causing scurvy with bleeding and poor wound healing.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 232–234.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: What are the two types of dietary iron?
questions.explanation: Dietary iron is classified as heme and nonheme; their food sources, absorption and sensitivity to meal inhibitors differ.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 261–265.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: A lack of iron can cause what condition?
questions.explanation: Progressive iron depletion can impair hemoglobin production and cause iron-deficiency anemia. Deficiency can exist before anemia develops.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 261–265.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: Zinc is needed for the activity of hundreds of:
questions.explanation: Zinc supports the catalytic activity of hundreds of enzymes and also has structural and regulatory functions.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 265–267.

questions.prompt: Iodine is a key part of which hormones?
questions.explanation: Iodine is incorporated into thyroxine and triiodothyronine; the other listed hormones do not contain iodine.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 267–268.

questions.prompt: The earliest clinical sign of iodine deficiency is usually:
questions.explanation: Goiter is a classic visible sign of iodine deficiency caused by thyroid stimulation. Deficiency may be subclinical before goiter is visible, so earliest is a teaching simplification.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 267–268.
questions.note: Printed answer supplied in the downloaded retake document; not authenticated as an official university answer key.

questions.prompt: Feeding through GI has been shown to:
questions.explanation: Appropriate enteral nutrition uses a functioning gastrointestinal tract and can support gut integrity and attenuate catabolism. It does not eliminate catabolism or guarantee better outcomes in every patient.
evidence: DeBruyne, Pinna & Whitney, Nutrition & Diet Therapy, 9th ed. (2016), PDF pp. 471–482.
